name: Spanish Empire

fields.foundation: The Spanish Empire is often described as the first global empire in history. It was built very quickly after two events: the dynastic union of the crowns of Castile and Aragon under Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon, complete from 1479, and the conclusion of the Reconquista with the fall of Granada in January 1492. Columbus's first voyage, sponsored by the Castilian crown and departing in August 1492, began the most consequential sequence of territorial acquisitions in imperial history. The empire's legal and political foundations were set out in the papal bulls of 1493, above all Inter caetera, which assigned Spain the right to lands discovered to the west, and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494), which fixed the meridian dividing the Spanish and Portuguese spheres. The conquest of Mexico by Hernán Cortés (1519–1521) and of Peru by Francisco Pizarro from 1532 turned Spain from a Caribbean colonial power into the master of the two wealthiest indigenous states of the Americas, and brought the gold and silver of the Aztec and Inca treasuries into the Spanish imperial system. Charles I of Spain, who already held the Burgundian Netherlands, inherited Castile and Aragon in 1516 and, as Charles V, the Austrian Habsburg lands and the imperial title in 1519, creating the first truly intercontinental political system in history. Under Philip II (r. 1556–1598) the empire reached its greatest extent, adding Portugal and its global network of trading posts and colonies through the dynastic union of 1580. The Spanish crown then ruled territories in Europe, the Americas, Africa, the Indian Ocean and the Pacific at once: the first 'empire on which the sun never sets.'
fields.socioeconomy: The Spanish imperial economy was built on the extraction and transatlantic transfer of American silver and gold. This brought the crown a fiscal windfall on a scale not seen before, and at the same time created the dependency that would prove the empire's long-term economic weakness. The silver mines of Potosí in Upper Peru (modern Bolivia), worked largely by indigenous labourers conscripted under the mita draft, and those of Zacatecas in Mexico, worked mainly by indigenous wage labour, made Spanish America the source of perhaps four-fifths of the world's silver between 1500 and 1800. The silver changed global monetary systems and funded Spanish military ambitions across three continents. The Casa de Contratación in Seville, founded in 1503, regulated colonial trade through a monopoly that channelled American silver through a single Castilian port. The monopoly generated customs revenue but also bottlenecks, smuggling and corruption, and it excluded foreigners and merchants of other Spanish ports from direct trade. The flood of silver passed through Spain into European financial systems, above all through repayments to the Genoese and German bankers who financed Habsburg campaigns, and contributed to the Price Revolution, a sustained sixteenth-century inflation that damaged Spanish agriculture and manufacturing relative to northern European competitors. The encomienda system extracted labour and tribute from indigenous populations, while the hacienda later emerged as the dominant form of landholding. The empire's commercial reach was wide: the Manila Galleon linked Acapulco and Manila from 1565 to 1815, the first sustained direct commercial link between the Americas and Asia. But a fiscal and mercantile policy that put extraction before production hindered the development of the domestic manufacturing and banking capacity that underpinned Dutch and British commercial wealth.
fields.military: The Spanish military of the sixteenth century was the strongest in Europe. It had been shaped by the long warfare of the Reconquista, the tactical lessons of the Italian Wars under commanders such as Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, 'the Great Captain', and the combination of firearms with disciplined formation warfare. Spanish infantry, victorious at Pavia (1525) and organised from 1534 into tercios combining pikemen and arquebusiers, gave Spain military dominance over its European opponents for more than a century, a reputation that was badly dented by defeat at Rocroi in 1643. In the Americas, Spanish firepower alone did not conquer the Aztec and Inca empires. The conquest depended on a combination of disease, above all smallpox, to which indigenous Americans had no prior exposure, the exploitation of indigenous rivalries and alliances, such as Cortés's alliance with Tlaxcala, and the shock of horses, firearms and steel weapons. Spanish sea power was shown at Lepanto (1571), where Spanish galleys formed a major part of the Holy League fleet that defeated the Ottomans, but the Armada sent against England in 1588 was defeated by English ships and wrecked by storms on the voyage home round Scotland and Ireland. Spain maintained forces simultaneously in Flanders, Italy, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, and this overextension imposed fiscal demands that silver revenues could not sustain. The crown was driven into repeated bankruptcies, or suspensions of payments, including those of 1557, 1575, 1596, 1607, 1627 and 1647, which undermined long-term military capacity. The Army of Flanders, which fought the Dutch Revolt from 1568 to 1648, consumed resources on a scale that permanently weakened Spanish military primacy.
fields.governance: The Spanish Empire developed the first comprehensive legal and administrative framework for overseas colonial government. It set precedents that shaped later European colonialism and, through the debates it generated, contributed to the emergence of international law. The Council of the Indies, established in 1524, governed the American colonies from Castile, and the colonial legislation it oversaw was later gathered in the Recopilación de Leyes de los Reinos de las Indias (1680), a comprehensive code covering every aspect of colonial administration. The viceroyalties of New Spain (1535) and Peru (1542) were the primary administrative units, later joined by New Granada (1717, re-established 1739) and Río de la Plata (1776), each headed by a viceroy of high rank who exercised near-royal authority subject to the oversight of the audiencias (colonial high courts) and the Council of the Indies. Spanish debates over the legitimacy of conquest were unusually intense. The Dominican friar Bartolomé de las Casas's campaign against the abuse of indigenous peoples helped produce the New Laws of 1542, which sought, with mixed success, to curb the encomienda and outlaw the enslavement of indigenous Americans, and in the Valladolid debate of 1550–1551 he argued against Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda's justification of conquest. The Church was a primary instrument of colonial rule: the Patronato Real gave the crown the right to nominate bishops and clergy in the colonies, making the ecclesiastical hierarchy an arm of the state that converted indigenous populations, educated colonial subjects and upheld social order. Corruption was endemic at every level of this structure, and the distances from Madrid to Lima or Manila meant that royal instructions often arrived months or years after the situations that prompted them had already changed.
fields.impact: No other state of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries changed the world as much as the Spanish Empire, which altered the demographic, ecological, economic and cultural geography of several continents at once. The Columbian Exchange, the transfer of crops, animals, pathogens and peoples between the Old World and the Americas, was the most consequential and irreversible result of the empire's expansion. American crops including maize, the potato, the tomato, cassava and the sweet potato changed nutrition across Europe, Africa and Asia, enabling population growth that would not otherwise have been possible. Eurasian diseases including smallpox, measles and typhus killed an estimated 50 to 90 per cent of the pre-contact indigenous population within a century of contact, one of the most catastrophic demographic events in human history. American silver disrupted monetary systems from Spain to China, where the Ming economy's growing reliance on silver created an enormous demand that the Manila Galleon trade helped to satisfy. The imposition of Catholic Christianity across the Americas, through missionary conversion, institutional coercion and the destruction of pre-Columbian religious sites, permanently changed the religious character of Latin America. The Spanish language, spread by imperial rule, is today official in some twenty countries. The debates about the legal and moral status of indigenous peoples prompted by the conquest contributed to the emergence of international law through the School of Salamanca, above all Francisco de Vitoria, whose ideas were later developed by Hugo Grotius.
fields.decline: The Spanish Empire declined slowly and unevenly: it lost military and commercial primacy in Europe decades before it began to lose territory in the Americas. The defeat of the Armada in 1588, while not strategically decisive in itself, marked the failure of direct maritime confrontation with England and the opening of northern European competition for Atlantic commercial supremacy. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648, in which the Treaty of Münster recognised Dutch independence after eighty years of the most expensive war in Spanish imperial history, confirmed Spain's loss of hegemony in northern Europe, and the Peace of the Pyrenees (1659) acknowledged the ascendancy of France. The War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) brought the Bourbon dynasty to the Spanish throne but cost Spain its Italian and Netherlandish possessions under the Utrecht settlement. The eighteenth-century Bourbon reforms sought to rationalise colonial administration, increase fiscal extraction from the Americas and build a more efficient military establishment. They had partial success, as colonial revenues rose substantially, but they also deepened creole resentment. That resentment fuelled independence movements after Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 displaced the Bourbon monarchy and destroyed the legitimacy that had held the colonial system together. The Spanish American wars of independence (1808–1826) dissolved the mainland American empire quickly, leaving Spain with Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines among its remaining major colonies. In the Spanish-American War of 1898 the United States destroyed Spanish squadrons at Manila Bay and Santiago de Cuba within months and stripped Spain of these last major overseas possessions, although small African territories remained. The dissolution had begun nearly a century earlier. The empire's four-century duration, global reach and cultural impact nonetheless make it one of the most consequential political enterprises in human history.
fields.summary: The Spanish Empire's greatest historical legacy is the Columbian Exchange, the irreversible biological, demographic and cultural transformation of the planet that followed its American conquests. Without intending it, the Spanish crown became the architect of the modern world's demographic geography.
fields.teaser: Often called the first global empire, Spain conquered the Aztec and Inca states and opened the Americas to European colonisation. Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas financed Habsburg wars and transformed the global economy.
fields.t0: Often called the first global empire, Spain ruled lands across Europe, the Americas, Africa and Asia from the 1490s.
fields.t1: American silver from mines like Potosí reshaped world money, and the Columbian Exchange transformed diets, populations and faiths.
fields.t2: Costly wars and bankruptcies eroded its power; the American colonies broke away by 1826 and the last major ones were lost in 1898.
fields.dyk: From 1565 to 1815 the Manila Galleon linked Acapulco and Manila, the first sustained direct trade link between the Americas and Asia.
